review_notes: The file has a single theorem, exact_law. I read all of it, then read MarginalRounding.lean (second_fractional, nonfractional_integral, exists_law), SparseCardinalRounding.lean, and the header of WeightedRounding.lean to look for repeated proof machinery. I found one real repetition: the step from a 0/1-valued vector with sum K to the selected set having card K. It appears in exact_law and in MarginalRounding.exists_law, and again over ℚ in SparseCardinalRounding. I did not report the second_fractional/nonfractional "fractional set is empty" argument as a finding. It is also repeated in SparseCardinalRounding.integral_of_small_fractional, but the two copies differ (exact_law has a card-contradiction via omega, the sparse one a ℚ-to-ℝ transfer). Nothing was compiled. Uncertainty: the proposed lemma is untested. I did not check whether ExactRounding imports MarginalRounding directly. It does use MarginalRounding.second_fractional, so the import must be transitive. Indicator is defined in WeightedRounding.lean, so its unfolding to `if i ∈ S then 1 else 0` should be definitional.

findings.excerpt:
have he : ((S ω).card:ℝ)=∑ i, Q ω i := by
      calc
        _ = ∑ i, indicator (S ω) i := by simp only [indicator,sum_boole,filter_univ_mem]
        _ = _ := sum_congr rfl (fun i _ => hbit ω hω i)
findings.problem: This block proves a general fact: if q : I → ℝ takes only the values 0 and 1 and sums to K, then S = univ.filter (q · = 1) has card K, and the indicator of S equals q pointwise. The same argument is written out again in MarginalRounding.exists_law (the `hpoint` and `hcard` blocks): rcases on `q i = 0 ∨ q i = 1`, then a calc `(S.card:ℝ) = ∑ i, if i ∈ S then 1 else 0 = ∑ i, q i`, then exact_mod_cast against hsum. SparseCardinalRounding.selected_indicator and selected_card repeat it a third time over ℚ. Each copy re-proves the pointwise indicator identity and the sum_boole/sum_congr cardinality calculation.
findings.proposed_change: Add one lemma to MarginalRounding.lean, next to nonfractional_integral and second_fractional (the file is already imported transitively, since exact_law uses second_fractional). Statement: `theorem binary_filter_spec {q : I → ℝ} {K : ℕ} (hq : ∀ i, q i = 0 ∨ q i = 1) (hsum : ∑ i, q i = K) : (∀ i, (if i ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun j => q j = 1) then (1:ℝ) else 0) = q i) ∧ (Finset.univ.filter (fun j => q j = 1)).card = K`. Proof sketch: for the first part, `rcases hq i with h | h <;> simp [h]`. For the second, `Finset.card_filter`/`sum_boole` give `(card:ℝ) = ∑ i, if … then 1 else 0`. Rewrite with `sum_congr` and the first part to get `∑ q = K`, then `exact_mod_cast`. Use in exact_law: for ω in the support, obtain `⟨hind, hc⟩ := binary_filter_spec (hint ω hω) (hsumq ω hω)`. Then `hbit ω hω i := hind i` (indicator unfolds definitionally to the `if`) and `hcard ω hω := hc`, which replaces lines 36-45. Use in exists_law: in the `hempty` branch, `have hbin := fun i => nonfractional_integral hq0 hq1 (hnot i)`, then `binary_filter_spec hbin hsum` supplies `hpoint` and `hcard` (lines 172-183). The ℚ copy in SparseCardinalRounding could reuse it via realPoint, or the lemma could be generalized to a linearly ordered field.
findings.benefit: The cardinality and indicator argument lives in one place and is proved once. exact_law and exists_law each shrink by about ten lines to a single call. Readers no longer have to check that the sum_boole/sum_congr calculations in separate files are the same, and any change to how the selected set is defined is made once.
